title: The April Evening Thomas Burberry's Basingstoke Shop Burned
dek: In April 1905 a window fire gutted Thomas Burberry's Basingstoke shop; he kept trading across the street and rebuilt on the same site.

story.event: The Winchester Street shop fire in Basingstoke and the decision to keep trading and rebuild on the same site
story.summary: On 17 April 1905 a fire started in the front window of Thomas Burberry's draper's and house-furnishing shop in Winchester Street, Basingstoke, and gutted the store and much of the street, causing about £30,000 of damage with no deaths. Burberry, whose gabardine cloth had by then made the firm known well beyond the town, traded from a shop opposite for about 17 months and opened a larger store on the same site in August 1906. Most records of the business's early years were probably lost in the fire.
paragraphs: At about five to six on the evening of 17 April 1905, a young assistant in the front window of Thomas Burberry's draper's and furnishing shop on Winchester Street, Basingstoke, set the display alight. The Basingstoke Gazette's account says she knocked over a gas lamp; the Hampshire Archives Trust says she was lighting the window with a taper. Within minutes the window was ablaze. Staff and customers were evacuated, and the town's brigade arrived quickly, but its steam pump drew only a trickle from the hydrants and the hoses leaked. At about half past six the roof fell in.

Burberry had seen this coming once. In December 1890 an assistant lighting a gaslight with a taper had touched the window stock; a colleague put it out with a bucket of water, and Burberry warned his staff that, in a shop full of flammable goods, another such accident could destroy the whole building. By 1905 the shop was only one part of his business. He had developed gabardine, a breathable cloth proofed in the yarn rather than coated in rubber, which the company dates to 1879 and says was patented in 1888. He had factories in the town and a base in London's West End.

Brigades from Winchester and Andover ran hoses down to the River Loddon, and the fire was out in the early hours. Most of the north side of Winchester Street was gutted, including an ironmonger's and John Mares's clothing factory. The damage was put at about £30,000. No one died.

Burberry, then about seventy, did not let the fire end his shopkeeping. For some 17 months he traded from a shop across the street, and in August 1906 a larger, more modern store opened on the old site; commemorative mugs show the shop before and after. The fire had a quieter cost. Historians think most records of the firm's early years were probably lost in it, and only one photograph of him seems to survive. That is partly why the story of how gabardine began, from talking to shepherds about their weatherproof smocks, cannot be checked.

quote.text: The tea-room is made for the tea master, not the tea-master for the tea-room. It is not intended for posterity and is therefore ephemeral.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Okakura's tea-room is built for the person who uses it, not for posterity. Burberry's shop burned with most of the firm's early papers, yet he went on serving customers from a room across the street. The business lived in the shopkeeper more than in the building.

reflection: Burberry had warned his staff fifteen years before, and it still happened. None of the accounts blames the young woman in the window. Some losses come despite the warning, and what he did next was ordinary: take the shop across the road and keep serving people while the new one went up.

The fire also took the papers that might have told us how his best idea began. Records matter, and you keep them for good reasons. But much of what makes your work good lives in people, not files: in how you and your colleagues actually do things. If it lives in only one head, that is a building with one exit.
invitation: Choose one thing at work that only you know how to do. Spend five minutes today showing one colleague how you do it, so it no longer lives in one place.

sources.title: Flashback: Burberry destroyed by fire in Basingstoke (27 April 2025)
sources.supports: The small window fire of 18 December 1890 (assistant lighting a gaslight with a taper, put out with a bucket of water) and Burberry's warning to staff; the fire at about 5.55pm on 17 April 1905 after an assistant knocked over a gas lamp in the window; evacuation of staff and customers; steam pump and hydrants yielding only a trickle, leaking pipes; roof falling in at 6.30pm; Winchester and Andover brigades pumping from the River Loddon; the fire out in the early hours; most of the north side of Winchester Street gutted, including Wagstaffe's ironmonger's and John Mares's clothing factory; about £30,000 of damage and no lives lost; Burberry trading from a shop opposite for 17 months until a larger, more modern store opened on the site in August 1906

sources.title: An international business sparked by a Hampshire shepherd (Thomas Burberry)
sources.supports: Thomas Burberry (1835-1926); gabardine woven in Lancashire and made up in Basingstoke factories; the perhaps apocryphal story that the idea came from talking to shepherds about their weatherproof smocks; Burberry retaining his Basingstoke retail business as the company grew in London; the fire of 17 April 1905 started when milliner Miss Gray tried to light the front window with a taper, the whole building gutted and the steam pump unequal to the task; the fire not deterring him from shopkeeping; most early business records probably destroyed in the fire; only one photograph of Burberry surviving and virtually no personal records

cross_checks.claim: On 17 April 1905 a fire that began in the shop window gutted Burberry's Winchester Street shop
The fire brigade's steam pump could not deliver enough water
A new Burberry shop opened on the site in 1906
Burberry kept his Basingstoke retail business while the firm grew in London
Gabardine is dated to 1879 and was patented in 1888
The shepherds' smock origin of gabardine is unverified legend

research_notes: Change of episode: the slate asked for the invention of gabardine in 1879, but no source documents the moment, the decision or what Burberry knew: the Hampshire Archives Trust says the shepherd story is perhaps apocryphal, that most early records were probably destroyed in the 1905 fire and that there are virtually no personal records; Sotheby's calls the smock inspiration legend. The edition therefore tells the well-documented 1905 Winchester Street fire (a setback) and keeps gabardine as background. Cause of the fire: the Basingstoke Gazette says an assistant knocked over a gas lamp in the window; the Hampshire Archives Trust says milliner Miss Gray tried to light up the window with a taper; the story gives both. Gabardine dates: Burberry plc and Sotheby's date the invention to 1879 and the patent to 1888; the Hampshire Cultural Trust and the Smock Shock blog say he patented it in 1879; Grace's Guide (quoting an older corporate profile) gives 1880; the story attributes 1879 and 1888 to the company. London: the Hampshire Cultural Trust dates a London outlet to 1891, while the Hampshire Archives Trust puts the move to London at the turn of the century; the story says only that he had a West End base by 1905. Basingstoke start: Burberry plc and the Hampshire Cultural Trust date the shop to 1856, while VCH dates his first factory to 1868 and the Gazette says he came to Basingstoke in 1868 to start a clothing firm; the story does not depend on either. The '17 months' is the Gazette's figure; from April 1905 to August 1906 is about 16 months, so the story says 'some 17 months'. Age: born 1835 (Hampshire Archives Trust), so about 69 or 70 at the fire; the story says 'about seventy'. The Gazette piece was published online on 27 April 2025 and says 'one hundred years ago', so it was probably first written for the 2005 centenary; its page carries a stray syndication notice that does not fit the local nostalgia content. VCH Explore is cited from the Institute of Historical Research's archived copy on GitHub Pages because the original site now redirects. Wikipedia's claim that Burberry founded the 1878 ready-to-wear factory conflicts with VCH, which credits his associates Gerrish and Ames; that detail is not used. Okakura wrote in English, so no translator is given; he is writing about the tea-room, and the passage is applied by analogy.
